Read the complete solution and reasoning

Linear-probing estimates are 12(1+10)=5.5 for hits and 12(1+100)=50.5 for misses. The ideal permutation miss bound is ten. Chaining under independent uniform homes gives 0.9 expected record comparisons for an absent query, plus constant hash/bucket work. These are not competing answers to one unqualified question; they describe different data structures, counters and random models. Linear probing pays for primary clustering. A chained miss may examine no records, while open addressing always examines at least its first slot. The assumptions and counter definitions must accompany every numerical value.

Question 62. Inverting a linear-probing miss budget

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

Under the standard asymptotic linear-probing estimate, require average misses of at most five probes. Solve for an allowed load and state why the conclusion is not a deterministic promise.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Solve 12(1+(1-α)-2)≤5, giving (1-α)-2≤9. For 0≤α<1, this yields 1-α≥1/3, hence α≤2/3. It is a design choice based on an asymptotic random-home insertion model. A specific table at that load can still have a long cluster and larger exact miss average; an adversarial key set can cause linear individual queries. Tombstones and deletions also change the applicable model. The bound is useful for planning expected performance while retaining the original assumptions, not certifying every operation.

Question 63. A chained-query budget

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

Universality gives absent-query expectation at most 900/m, so m≥300 suffices. At capacity 300, a present fixed key's expected bucket size is at most 1+899/300=1199/300, just below four. This is an upper bound on scanning the complete bucket, not necessarily the exact successful rank. Load three is valid for chaining and can satisfy this record-comparison budget despite exceeding one. Hash evaluation, equality costs and any dynamic rebuilding add separately. Incremental growth scans old capacities one through 63, totaling 63·64/2=2016. Doubling scans old capacities 1,2,4,8,16,32, totaling 63. The final allocated capacity is 64 in both comparisons; it is not another old-capacity scan in this setup. Initialization of the new arrays also forms a geometric linear sum for doubling, while incremental growth remains quadratic. Collision and key-processing work must still be justified separately. This aggregate capacity arithmetic explains the resize policy's amortized benefit, without asserting that an individual triggering insertion takes constant time.

Question 67. Hysteresis and oscillation

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

A table doubles when full and halves whenever live load falls to one-half. Construct an alternating-update sequence causing repeated linear rebuilds, and give a safer threshold separation.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Start with a full capacity- m table. An insertion triggers growth to 2m and leaves m+1 entries. Deleting one returns to m entries, exactly half load, triggering shrink to m. Repeating insertion and deletion causes a rebuild every operation, each scanning a linear number of records. Shrinking instead near one-quarter load creates a gap: after growth, many deletions are needed before shrink, and after shrink, many insertions are needed before growth. Precise thresholds depend on the collision strategy, but they must prevent immediate oscillation. Geometric capacity changes alone do not guarantee amortized constant updates with badly chosen shrink rules.

Question 68. Duplicate updates and live count

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

A table grows only when inserting a new key would exceed its live-load threshold. It receives 1000 put operations all on the same key. How many records should exist, and why can checking size before distinguishing updates cause unnecessary growth?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The map has one live record after the first insertion. Each later operation replaces its value and leaves live count unchanged. A correct threshold policy should avoid treating those updates as additional entries. Checking a conservative threshold before search can be functionally correct but may rebuild unnecessarily if an existing key would not raise the count. The interface's semantics determine which count changes are legitimate. A frequency map follows the same rule: many occurrences update one entry rather than creating duplicate records. Expected update search still depends on the bucket or probe route; repeated key identity does not justify arbitrary counter increments.

Question 69. One-level perfect-hashing probability

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

Twelve fixed keys use a universal family with capacity 122. Bound the probability of any collision and expected independent trials until collision-free placement. Separate test work from dense-array initialization.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Expected collision pairs are at most (122)/144=11/24. Markov gives collision-event probability at most 11/24, so success probability is at least 13/24. Expected independent trials are at most 24/13, below two. Testing twelve placements can be linear in the key count using suitable sparse or timestamped machinery, but initializing all 144 slots costs that capacity. As n grows, the one-level n2 table uses quadratic space and potentially quadratic initialization work. The probability calculation alone does not establish an overall linear-space or dense-array linear-time construction.

Question 70. A two-level allocation calculation

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

A first-level perfect-hashing attempt has six buckets with lengths [3,0,1,2,0,0]. Compute total second-level slots, collision pairs and the 4n acceptance test. Include empty buckets explicitly.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The live count is six. Squared lengths sum to 9+0+1+4=14, so the second-level arrays require fourteen slots before constant metadata. Pair collisions in first-level buckets are three plus one, totaling four, and the identity n+2P=6+8=14 checks the result. Since 4n=24, this attempt passes the stated first-level space test. Bucket zero's three records require their own nine-slot collision-free second level; skipping index zero would lose half the keys. Empty buckets need no second-level record array, but queries reaching them must return absence safely.

Exact deterministic companion for the stated inputs and declared operation. Read the saved state to distinguish intermediate repair from completed lookup invariants.

Q68: bucket zero and fourteen second-level slots

Match the declared hash context, exact probe route and slot/bucket state. Only completed checkpoints certify a completed operation.

Question 71. Two-level expected squared space

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

For n fixed keys and a universal first-level hash into n buckets, derive an upper bound on expected squared bucket lengths and the probability that this sum exceeds 4n.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The squared sum equals n+2P where P is the unordered first-level collision-pair count. Universality gives E[P]≤(n2)/n=(n-1)/2, hence expected squared sum at most 2n-1. Markov gives probability of a sum exceeding 4n at most (2n-1)/(4n)<1/2. Therefore independent first-level retries have success probability above one-half under this acceptance policy. The expected value is a bound, not necessarily an equality, because universal families can have smaller pair probabilities. Accepted final second-level allocation is deterministically at most 4n for this test, while the number of construction trials remains randomized.

Question 72. Perfect lookup still verifies the key

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

A static perfect table has no collisions among its stored keys. Explain why an absent query must compare the key in its computed candidate slot and why inserting a new key can invalidate the guarantee.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Perfectness concerns only the known stored set. An outside key can hash to the same two-level location as a stored record, so treating any occupied candidate as a match would return a false value. Compare the actual key after the two hash computations and report absence if unequal. A new key may collide with existing second-level placement; the original construction's acceptance tests did not include it. Supporting arbitrary dynamic insertion therefore requires rebuilding affected structure or a separately analyzed dynamic-perfect scheme. Worst-case constant slot lookup after successful static construction is a distinct claim from dynamic update costs or full-universe injectivity.

Question 73. Geometric trial expectation

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

Every independent perfect-hashing trial succeeds with probability at least one-half. Bound expected trials and the probability more than six trials are needed. Explain how lack of fresh randomness changes the conclusion.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

With success probability p≥1/2, the expected geometric trial count is 1/p≤2. Needing more than six trials means six consecutive failures, with probability at most (1/2)6=1/64 under fresh independent choices, or under appropriately conditioned per-trial failure bounds. Reusing the same failed hash function gives the same placement, so repeated attempts are not independent trials and can fail forever. The expectation is not a deadline guarantee; rare long sequences remain possible. Recording the successful parameters makes final lookup deterministic even though construction used random retries.

Question 74. Initialization included in perfect construction

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

An accepted two-level first stage has ∑jℓj2≤4n. Each nonempty bucket needs at most two expected trials, each initializing and checking ℓj2 slots. Derive total expected second-stage work including initialization.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For each bucket, expected work is at most a fixed constant times 2ℓj2, absorbing placement/checking of its ℓj records because ℓj≤ℓj2 when nonempty. Sum over buckets to get at most a constant times 2(4n)=8n. This is linear expected total work and includes dense second-level initialization, unlike an unqualified one-level n2 construction claim. Empty buckets contribute only bounded first-level metadata work. The accepted first-level space condition is crucial; without it the squared sum could be quadratic. Random construction and deterministic post-construction lookup remain separately stated properties.

Question 75. Bloom-filter false positives

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

A Bloom filter has 1000 bits, stores 100 keys and uses seven ideal independent bit hashes. Estimate false-positive probability and explain why this is not an exact dictionary membership result.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The continuous estimate of a zero bit is e-700/1000=e-0.7. Approximate occupied-bit fraction is 1-e-0.7≈0.5034, giving false-positive estimate (1-e-0.7)7≈0.0082. Exact zero-bit probability under independent draws is (999/1000)700, but treating queried bit events as independent is an additional approximation. A positive response only means all requested bits are set, not that the key was inserted. Under an insertion-only correct implementation, an inserted key has no false negative because its bits remain set. Clearing shared bits for deletion breaks that property.

The thirteen-bit mechanism demonstration uses explicitly declared deterministic bit functions. It is not a numerical visualization of the ideal 1000-bit probability calculation.

Bit sharing and a possible false-positive query

Match the declared hash context, exact probe route and slot/bucket state. Only completed checkpoints certify a completed operation.

Question 76. The Bloom-filter optimum

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

For bit budget b and n keys, state the approximate optimum number of hashes and compute it when b/n=8. Compare the two neighboring integers and explain the computational tradeoff.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The standard continuous false-positive approximation is minimized near k=(b/n)ln2. At ratio eight this is about 5.545, so test integer choices five and six under the chosen approximation. They give roughly (1-e-5/8)5≈0.0217 and (1-e-6/8)6≈0.0216, with six slightly better. Every additional hash also adds work, so a practical choice can trade a small probability difference for throughput. The optimum is not a universal exact theorem for correlated hash outputs or a fixed finite bit layout. It depends on the idealized model and the absence of deletion errors.

Question 77. A cuckoo capacity obstruction

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

Four keys have candidate pairs drawn only from three slots: (A,B),(B,C),(A,C),(A,B). Prove no one-key-per-slot placement exists. Does one cycle alone always imply failure?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The four distinct keys have only three available candidate slots in their connected component. Pigeonhole immediately rules out placement. In the candidate graph, this component has four edges and three vertices, so it contains more keys than positions. A component containing exactly one cycle can still place its keys by orienting that cycle consistently and attaching tree edges away from it. Therefore observing a displacement cycle can indicate failure of a particular insertion path or trigger a bounded rebuilding policy without proving that every possible placement is impossible. The four-on-three example is a genuine structural obstruction, not merely an animation loop.

The compact three-key example has candidate positions L0 and R0 for each key, so three records cannot fit in two positions. This illustrates the same candidate-set obstruction with different inputs.

Three keys competing for two candidate positions

Match the declared hash context, exact probe route and slot/bucket state. Only completed checkpoints certify a completed operation.

Question 78. Two-sum with duplicate values

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

Process [4,1,4] for target eight using a prior-values hash set. Give the exact query/insert sequence and explain why inserting before querying can produce a wrong answer for input [4].

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Initially the set is empty. For the first four, query complement four and miss, then insert four. For one, query seven and miss, then insert one. For the final four, query four and succeed because the first position already supplied that value. Two distinct positions form the pair. If the current value were inserted before its own complement query, the one-element input four would falsely match itself. The set stores values rather than positions, but the operation order enforces distinctness. Expected linear total work follows only with the table's expected lookup/insertion assumptions and safe arithmetic for computing the complement.

Question 79. Prefix-sum counting

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

Count zero-sum contiguous subarrays of [2,-2,2,-2] using a frequency map of prior prefix sums. Give every update and total, including the initial empty prefix.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Start frequencies with zero occurring once. The prefix sums are two, zero, two and zero. At prefix two, add its prior frequency zero and set its count to one. At zero, add one and raise zero's count to two. At the next two, add one and raise two's count to two. At the final zero, add two and raise zero's count to three. Total is four. The empty-prefix initialization counts subarrays starting at the first element. Query before incrementing prevents counting a zero-length subarray at the current position. Map updates replace counts; they do not create duplicate key records.

Question 80. Ordered queries versus equality queries

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

A service needs equality lookup, predecessor by key, key median and deletion of maximum priority, with priority unrelated to key order. Explain why one plain hash table is insufficient and outline a correct combined structure.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

A hash table routes by equality-oriented codes and does not preserve key or priority order. Predecessor and median cannot be inferred from neighboring physical slots. Maintain a balanced tree ordered by key with subtree sizes for rank selection and an aggregate identifying the maximum-priority record under a specified tie policy. An identifier map can locate records quickly. Priority changes update winner aggregates along the affected path; deletion changes both size and priority metadata. All mutation paths must maintain consistency. With balanced height, the ordered operations and aggregate maintenance take logarithmic worst-case tree work; hash lookup contributes its separately qualified expected cost.

The Robin Hood companion illustrates displacement exchange. The prompt asks for a multi-operation ordered dictionary design, whose proof is given in the written solution.

Question 81. A deterministic alternative under hostile hashing

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

An application requires a worst-case logarithmic bound for arbitrary keys and ordered range queries. Should an expected constant-time chained table automatically be preferred? Give a justified selection.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The requirements favor a balanced comparison tree with an appropriate key comparison operation. It supports ordered range/rank navigation and has a logarithmic worst-case height guarantee. A chained table may have faster typical equality lookup but permits a linear bucket and does not supply ordered range navigation. Combining structures can support both, yet adds memory and consistency work. The choice depends on required operations and guarantees rather than comparing unqualified “one” versus “logarithm” costs. If key comparisons inspect long strings, the tree's character cost must also be stated; worst-case node visits and total key-processing work are distinct measures.

Question 82. A complete counter-and-correctness audit

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original or independently reconstructed written-course exercise family; numerical data and complete reasoning authored for this chapter.

Audit this claim: “At load below one-half, every hash-map insertion is constant worst-case time; any deleted slot can terminate search; resizing only copies slots; equal hashes identify equal keys.” Give a precise replacement for each clause.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Low load can support constant expected performance under a suitable random model but does not prevent concentrated chains or long linear-probing clusters. A deleted marker preserves reachability and must not terminate unsuccessful search; only a never-used/currently repaired empty slot provides that certificate. Resizing changes routes, so live records must be rehashed/reinserted and a triggering operation can be linear actual time. Equal hashes require an actual key-equality check; unequal keys can collide even with a good family. A valid map additionally handles duplicate updates without increasing live count and uses bounded routes. These corrections jointly restore both the contract and the cost qualifications rather than patching only one erroneous complexity label.

23. Final reasoning rules and examination traps

Final reasoning rules and examination traps

These rules supplement the derivations and worked problems. Read each condition before using its formula. A correct formula under the wrong probability model can produce an incorrect examination answer.

Rule 1

State whether the abstraction is a set, a map or a multimap. A map has one record per equality class, so putting an existing key updates its value and does not increase the live count. A multimap may intentionally retain several records with equal keys.

Rule 2

Hash equality is necessary for equal keys but insufficient to establish key equality. Two unequal keys can share a hash code or bucket; a successful lookup still requires the specified equality test.

Rule 3

Equality and hashing must refer to the same immutable key information. Changing that information after insertion can leave a record in a bucket that future lookups no longer visit. Rehashing after an authorized key change must repair the representation.

Rule 4

Normalize negative remainders explicitly. For positive capacity m, floor modulo produces a value in {0,…,m-1}; a language remainder operation can instead produce a negative value and cannot directly index the array safely.

Rule 5

Charge for evaluating the hash function. Hashing an uncached string of length L ordinarily requires Θ(L) character work even when the expected number of table probes is constant. Distinguish bit complexity from a fixed-word computational model.

Rule 6

Evaluate polynomial string hashes by Horner's rule: multiply the preceding residue by the base, add the next character code and reduce modulo m. This avoids storing large powers but does not make the function injective.

Rule 7

Arithmetic progressions can be pathological under modular hashing. Keys separated by a multiple of m share a home, even when their original numeric values look widely separated. Calculate residues before assuming a uniform distribution.

Rule 8

Ordinary comparison lower bounds for ordered searching do not prohibit expected constant-time dictionary operations using hashing. They refer to different operation models and different information available from a key.

Rule 9

Separate chaining permits n>m because a bucket stores a collection of records. Ordinary open addressing stores at most one live record per physical slot, so it requires n≤m and usually reserves substantial empty space.

Rule 10

Define n as the number of live records and m as the number of buckets or slots before computing α=n/m. A duplicate-key update changes neither n nor the live load.

Rule 11

A bucket with b live records requires b equality checks for an unsuccessful sequential search. Include the constant routing and bucket-access work if the question asks for total time rather than equality comparisons alone.

Rule 12

Head insertion reverses the insertion order within each separate chain. If a problem asks for the successful-search cost of a particular key, derive its actual chain position; its hash home alone does not give that cost.

Rule 13

A map insertion into a chain must normally check for an existing equal key. Concentrating n distinct insertions in one bucket gives n(n-1)/2 failed equality checks. Constant-time linking does not remove this quadratic uniqueness-checking work.

Rule 14

For a fixed table and uniformly chosen live key, successful chain comparisons average ∑jbj(bj+1)/(2n). This expression depends on the actual bucket sizes, not merely the total load.

Rule 15

For a fixed table and a uniformly chosen home, unsuccessful chain equality checks average n/m. This exact conditional calculation does not assert that arbitrary queries choose their homes uniformly.

Rule 16

The bucket containing a uniformly chosen live key is size-biased. Its expected size is ∑jbj2/n, whereas a uniformly chosen bucket has mean size n/m. Do not interchange these sampling procedures.

Rule 17

Under independent uniform placement, the expected number of occupied buckets is m[1-(1-1/m)n]. It counts nonempty buckets, not pair collisions or equality checks.

Rule 18

Under independent uniform placement, one bucket's occupancy is binomial with mean n/m and variance (n/m)(1-1/m). The expected value alone does not prove every bucket is short.

Rule 19

Count unordered colliding pairs using one indicator for each pair of distinct keys. When pair collision probability is 1/m, the expected count is n(n-1)/(2m) by linearity of expectation; mutual independence of the indicators is unnecessary.

Rule 20

Distinguish a total pair count from collisions involving one selected key. The latter has expectation (n-1)/m under the same pairwise assumptions. A factor of approximately n/2 separates the two quantities.

Rule 21

The birthday threshold concerns whether any pair collides. A table can have a low live load while the probability of at least one collision is already substantial; these are different events.

Rule 22

For n≤m independent uniform homes, the exact probability of no collision is ∏i=0n-1(1-i/m). If n>m, that probability is zero by the pigeonhole principle.

Rule 23

The exponential birthday expression is an approximation, not an identity. Its accuracy requires control of the higher-order terms in the logarithm of the exact product. Use the finite product when the problem supplies small exact parameters.

Rule 24

The union bound gives Pr(some collision)≤n(n-1)/(2m). A bound larger than one is uninformative rather than a valid probability value; probabilities remain at most one.

Rule 25

A universal hash family bounds the collision probability for each fixed distinct pair when the function is chosen randomly. It does not say that every function in the family distributes every input set evenly.

Rule 26

For affine hashing modulo prime p, choose the multiplier from the nonzero field elements and the offset from the entire field. Restricting both parameters to the smaller input range can destroy the collision guarantee.

Rule 27

Distinct input keys must first have distinct encodings in the declared prime-field universe. Reducing arbitrary unbounded integer keys modulo a fixed small prime can merge them before the affine family is applied.

Rule 28

For distinct field inputs, the affine parameter map produces a uniform ordered pair of distinct field outputs. Count outputs that reduce to the same bucket; this counting proof supplies the universal bound without assuming independent final bucket values.

Rule 29

Pairwise collision control is weaker than full independence. Use linearity of expectation for collision counts, but do not automatically apply a binomial distribution or an independent birthday product to a merely universal family.

Rule 30

State whether keys and queries are fixed before the random function is sampled. An adversary that learns the function and then chooses colliding keys can invalidate a guarantee proved for a fixed input set.

Rule 31

Open addressing uses the same complete deterministic route for insertion, lookup and deletion of a particular key in one table context. A lookup using another route has no reason to find a displaced record.

Rule 32

A key is reachable only if no earlier slot on its insertion route is currently EMPTY. This is the invariant that justifies stopping a lookup at an empty slot.

Rule 33

An EMPTY slot certifies absence along a correctly maintained route; a DELETED marker does not. A tombstone preserves the possibility that an equal key is stored farther along that route.

Rule 34

Count a terminating EMPTY inspection as a probe even though it performs no equality comparison with a live key. Similarly, visiting a tombstone increases probe count but need not increase key-equality count.

Rule 35

For linear probing, compute (h+i)modm for successive offsets. Remember wraparound from m-1 to zero; writing an unbounded sequence of array indices loses the circular structure.

Rule 36

A contiguous circular run of r occupied cells contributes r(r+1)/2 extra unsuccessful-search probes over uniformly chosen homes. Summing these terms yields the exact fixed-table miss average when at least one EMPTY slot exists.

Rule 37

Equal load factors do not imply equal linear-probing costs. A single long cluster and many isolated entries can have very different sums of squared run lengths. Use the actual arrangement if it is given.

Rule 38

Primary clustering attracts additional keys whose homes fall inside an existing run. This phenomenon follows from linear routing and should not be confused with unequal keys merely sharing their original home.

Rule 39

During insertion with tombstones, remember the first reusable marker and continue searching for an existing equal key. Committing at the marker immediately can create a duplicate map entry.

Rule 40

If an equal key is found beyond a tombstone, update its existing record. Neither a new live entry nor a tombstone reuse occurs; the marker remains available for another genuinely absent key.

Rule 41

If a full bounded route scan finds no duplicate but remembers a tombstone, insertion can reuse that marker. The absence of an EMPTY slot does not itself prove that no physical reusable slot exists.

Rule 42

Every probing loop needs a finite bound. A full table or a nonpermuting route can otherwise make an unsuccessful lookup loop forever. Report route exhaustion separately from successful insertion.

Rule 43

Tombstone occupancy affects search termination. A table with few live keys but many markers can have long misses; distinguish live load n/m from nonempty routing occupancy (n+d)/m.

Rule 44

Backward shifting is a linear-probing repair rule. For home h, hole u and current slot v, shift only when circular distance from h to u is strictly less than the distance from h to v.

Rule 45

A record already at its home must remain there when the repair hole lies later on its circular route. Mechanically shifting every encountered record can break reachability for mixed-home clusters.

Rule 46

The repair hole is temporary until the scan reaches the cluster boundary. Client lookups during an incomplete repair need an additional concurrency protocol; the sequential proof assumes the repair operation is completed atomically from their perspective.

Rule 47

The route h+i2modp visits exactly (p+1)/2 positions for odd prime p. It is not a permutation of all p slots, even though the modulus is prime.

Rule 48

For square probing at odd prime capacity, fewer than (p+1)/2 nonempty positions guarantee an empty position on each route. Tombstones count as nonempty for this guarantee; low live load alone is insufficient after many deletions.

Rule 49

Quadratic probing generally retains secondary clustering: keys with the same home use the same offset sequence. Eliminating contiguous linear runs does not eliminate every correlation between probe routes.

Rule 50

Alternating positive and negative squares give full coverage at primes congruent to three modulo four. The proof relies on minus one being a nonsquare; it does not apply to primes congruent to one modulo four.

Rule 51

Triangular offsets i(i+1)/2 form a permutation modulo a power of two over one full capacity-length route. Preserve the exact offset formula and the power-of-two capacity condition when using this result.

Rule 52

Double hashing uses h1(k)+is(k) modulo m. Its exact cycle length is m/gcd(s(k),m), so full coverage requires the step to be coprime with the capacity.

Rule 53

A step that does not divide the capacity need not be coprime with it. At capacity twelve, step eight does not divide twelve but visits only three slots; use the greatest common divisor test.

Rule 54

At prime capacity, every nonzero step modulo the capacity gives full coverage. At a power-of-two capacity, the valid full-cycle steps are precisely the odd residues.

Rule 55

Zero step revisits the home forever unless the loop has a finite bound. A negative step can give full coverage after modular normalization, but the same coprimality condition still applies.

Rule 56

Distinct homes or steps can produce distinct affine routes, yet double hashing samples far fewer routes than all m! permutations. Do not identify its deterministic route family with ideal uniform permutation probing.

Rule 57

In ideal uniform permutation probing with n<m occupied cells, an unsuccessful search has exact expectation (m+1)/(m-n+1). This finite formula includes the terminating empty inspection.

Rule 58

The familiar 1/(1-α) unsuccessful-search expression is an upper bound in the ideal model, not the exact finite expectation. For small capacities, the difference can be substantial.

Rule 59

The ideal successful-search average requires a stated insertion history and a uniformly chosen stored key. Average each key's insertion-time miss cost at its earlier occupancy; do not use the final-load miss cost for every key.

Rule 60

The logarithmic ideal successful-search bound and the classical linear-probing estimates come from different models. Always identify whether the question assumes random permutations or independent uniform linear-probing homes.

Rule 61

The classical linear-probing miss estimate grows approximately as half of (1-α)-2 near full load. The ideal permutation bound grows as (1-α)-1, illustrating why substituting one for the other can materially underestimate work.

Rule 62

An expected bound concerns randomness in a declared input or hashing model. It does not remove the deterministic linear worst case for one lookup or the possibility of a concentrated adversarial input.

Rule 63

Resizing changes the modulus and therefore the home of a key. Reinsert live records under the new context instead of copying physical old slots to equal array indices.

Rule 64

Preserve record identity, values and equality classes during rebuilding. Tombstones are discarded; live records must appear once each. A rebuild is not an ordinary insertion that creates additional user records.

Rule 65

Geometric capacity growth bounds the sum of allocation sizes by a geometric series. If rebuilding has expected linear cost under the stated model, this supports expected amortized constant update overhead.

Rule 66

One growth-triggering insertion can still take linear actual time. Expected, amortized and worst-case are separate qualifiers; an expected amortized bound does not prove a constant latency bound for every operation.

Rule 67

Use separated growth and shrink thresholds. Shrinking immediately after crossing the growth boundary can cause repeated expensive rebuilds on an alternating insert/delete sequence.

Rule 68

Cleanup decisions may depend on marker occupancy as well as live load. Rebuilding at the same capacity can remove tombstones and shorten routes without increasing the physical array size.

Rule 69

Perfect hashing is injective on a fixed known set, not necessarily on the whole universe. A candidate query still requires checking the stored key to reject an absent key mapped to the same position.

Rule 70

A universal one-level table with n2 positions has expected pair-collision count below one-half for n>1. Markov's inequality gives at least one-half probability of no collision, but dense initialization can still require quadratic work.

Rule 71

The identity ∑jbj2=n+2C relates squared bucket sizes to the number C of unordered colliding pairs. It is an exact identity for a fixed distribution, preceding any expectation calculation.

Rule 72

With approximately n first-level buckets and universal hashing, expected squared allocation is below 2n. Rejecting a first-level function when allocation exceeds 4n yields a constant acceptance probability by Markov's inequality.

Rule 73

Allocate bj2 second-level positions for a bucket containing bj fixed keys. Independently retry a universal second-level function until those keys are collision-free, and include bucket zero in the construction.

Rule 74

A constant expected number of trials requires fresh independent parameter choices and a lower-bounded success probability. A deterministic search in the compact laboratory illustrates valid placement but is not evidence for the randomized trial theorem.

Rule 75

A Bloom filter stores bits rather than key identities. All queried bits being set means possibly present; an unset bit certifies absence when insertions use the same functions and no unsafe bit clearing has occurred.

Rule 76

The common Bloom false-positive expression (1-e-kn/m)k is an approximation under a stated ideal hashing model. Choosing k near (m/n)ln2 minimizes that approximation; compare neighboring integer choices.

Rule 77

Cuckoo placement gives each key a small set of candidates. A set of keys with fewer total candidate positions than keys is impossible to place; a bounded failed relocation attempt does not itself prove impossibility for every candidate graph.

Rule 78

Robin Hood insertion prioritizes the more displaced record at a contested slot. Search and deletion rules must match that representation; importing tombstone or early-stopping rules from another policy requires a separate proof.

Rule 79

Hash tables support equality lookup rather than ordered statistics by themselves. Median, predecessor and range requests need additional order-maintaining structure or explicitly analyzed extra work.

Rule 80

Finish an examination solution by checking the exact event counted, load definition, route formula, marker policy, query distribution, computational model and complexity qualifier. A numeric answer without these conditions can conceal a different problem from the one stated.

24. Editable specialized laboratory

The compact laboratory accepts capacities two through thirteen and at most sixteen integer inputs between minus 999 and 999. Chaining uses at most eight inputs and eight buckets. Perfect placement requires distinct keys, at most three keys per bucket and four occupied buckets for readable second-level arrays. Rebuilding uses linear probing and enough new slots for every distinct key. Backward shifting requires a present deletion target and linear probing. Cuckoo placement uses distinct keys and declared candidate functions; bounded relocation failure is labeled. Robin Hood placement requires enough slots. Polynomial inputs are character codes; Bloom inputs use the explicit deterministic bit functions printed in the checkpoint. These mechanism samples do not simulate random hashing distributions. A probe route can exhaust before the physical table fills. Every trace starts paused, and invalid input preserves the preceding valid trace.
